deck: 30 Thinking in Java::05 Initialization and Cleanup

cards.front: Why does Java use a constructor instead of an initialize() method?
cards.back: So initialisation is guaranteed — nobody can create the object without it running
cards.extra: An ordinary method relies on the caller remembering to call it. The constructor runs before the new object can be used at all.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::07 Object Lifecycle

cards.front: What is unusual about a constructor's signature?
cards.back: It has the class's name and no return type at all — not even void
cards.extra: A return type would turn it into an ordinary method. That is why void Foo() in class Foo silently fails to initialise anything.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::07 Object Lifecycle

cards.front: A class defines only Tree(int height). Can you still build a Tree with no arguments?
cards.back: No — the constructor set is exactly what you declare
cards.extra: There is no implicit no-arg constructor once you write any constructor. Callers must supply the argument or you must add a second constructor.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::07 Object Lifecycle

cards.front: What does this refer to inside a method?
cards.back: The current object — the one the method was called on
cards.extra: It is how a method returns itself for chaining, and how a constructor calls a sibling constructor. Without it you could not tell a field from a parameter of the same name.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::07 Object Lifecycle

cards.front: When does an instance initialisation block run?
cards.back: Before the constructor body, after the fields are set to their defaults
cards.extra: Blocks execute in declaration order, every time an object is created. The book uses them for initialisation shared by several constructors.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::19 Initializer Block

cards.front: What is a static block for?
cards.back: One-time initialisation of class-level state, run when the class is loaded
cards.extra: It executes once, before any instance exists. That makes it the place for filling a static table or reading configuration that every instance will need.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::04 Static Keyword

cards.front: Can you rely on finalize() to clean up?
cards.back: No — the GC may never call it, and the book calls it unreliable
cards.extra: There is no guarantee of when, or whether, finalisation happens. Resources are released with explicit close/try-with-resources, not with finalize.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::07 Object Lifecycle

cards.front: What does final mean on a field?
cards.back: It can be assigned exactly once — at declaration or in a constructor
cards.extra: A blank final is the common pattern: final int id; set in the constructor. After that, assigning to it is a compile error.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::10 Final Keyword

cards.front: What happens if a constructor calls a method that a subclass overrides?
cards.back: The subclass version runs — before the subclass's fields are initialised
cards.extra: Late binding applies during construction too. The override sees default (0/null) values for fields the subclass has not set yet — a classic source of subtle bugs.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::14 Static vs Dynamic Binding
